Oil freight rates continue to climb, with the Persian Gulf to Far East benchmark hitting ~$1.4 million a day. It was less than $50,000 a day a year ago. The rally is spilling over many other routes far away from the Middle East conflict, particularly those from US GoM and WAF.

The first hurricane of the North Atlantic season: Isais, which has formed inside the US Gulf of Mexico. On current tracking forecast, the threat is limited to GoM oil production. Crucially, little refining capacity in Alabama (3 refineries in total, with ~140,000 of capacity).

For all the Iranian attacks against oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz since early October, loading activity inside the Persian Gulf remains very strong (and more ballast tankers coming in, even in daylight). Flows may become more lumpy, with larger day-on-day swings, but overall it looks like SoH crossing will carry on.

Further increases in oil freight rates today. 

The rally, which started in earnest in early September, is causing havoc in the physical crude market. It's inflating some benchmarks (Dated Brent, notably), but also forcing record discounts (WAF crude, in particular).

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says that it will block "soon" the "illegal" routes in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official Fars news agency. 

(effectively, the first public admission by the IRGC that the waterway isn't closed anymore)

Jet exports totalled 70 million barrels between January and July up from 45 million in the same period a year earlier. Highlights from the EIA’s weekly inventory report: 
US crude inventories fell by 3.2 million barrels last week to 424 million barrels, broadly in line with the seasonal average. SPR releases added 1.1 million barrels of supply, while US crude production rose to nearly 14 mb/d. Refinery crude demand increased by 223 kb/d to 16.5 mb/d, a seasonal record high, while higher imports and exports left net crude imports broadly unchanged.

Total US crude and fuel exports climbed to 12.8 mb/d, the highest since May and a seasonal record. Meanwhile, four-week average implied gasoline demand stood at 8.8 mb/d, roughly in line with the seasonal norm.

#Commodities:

Brent #crudeoil gained further ground, trading near USD 103, while WTI is back above USD 90 amid concerns the Middle East conflict could flare up again ahead of the US midterms after the White House reportedly asked the Pentagon to draw up strike options. Meanwhile, a storm in the Gulf of Mexico has forced the shutdown of around 500 kb/d of US production. Combined with recent attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, these developments underline just how far the global oil market remains from normalisation. Crude continues to be shipped at exceptionally high cost, while curtailed fuel exports are keeping product markets tight. Gasoil - the key pricing benchmark for diesel, jet fuel, marine and heating fuels - has climbed back above USD 191 per barrel.

#Gold trades back above USD 4,100 after briefly tumbling through support on Thursday as bond yields and the dollar climbed to fresh cycle highs. The price action highlights an ongoing battle between macro- and technically focused traders selling gold in response to higher funding costs and dollar strength, and investors seeking protection against the potential fiscal fallout from rising debt and borrowing costs. The latter remains evident in ETF demand, with total holdings reaching a fresh four-year high on Wednesday. Gains during today’s Asian session may also have been supported by the return of Chinese investors following the week-long Golden Week holiday. The gold-silver ratio trades near 70, a two-month high as ETF flows show investors currently favouring gold over #silver. 

#Copper rose alongside other metals as Chinese traders returned from a week-long holiday, restoring liquidity to Asian markets. Prices are also being supported by a strike at a major mine in Chile. More broadly, copper in London and New York has spent the past couple of months consolidating near record highs, underpinned by expectations for robust demand and persistent challenges in expanding mine supply. The longer-term demand outlook remains supported by several structural themes, including electrification, renewable energy, electric vehicles, grid expansion, and rapidly growing power demand from data centres.
